title: An Act relating to health insurance; to impose limitations on the use of artificial intelligence by insurers in making determinations of coverage (Act 2026-589)
regulatedParties: Health insurers and their contracted utilization review entities
keyRequirements: An insurer may not use AI as the sole basis to deny, reduce or defer health care services; any adverse determination based in whole or part on medical necessity must be made by a licensed physician or other competent health care professional. Insurers must disclose their use of AI in utilization review to enrollees. AI use in utilization review is subject to review by the Department of Insurance.
enforcement: Alabama Department of Insurance may investigate, require corrective action plans, and take disciplinary action; no private right of action stated
notes: Reported as Act 2026-589. Signing date confirmed via Transparency Coalition legislative update and JD Supra; the engrossed bill PDF does not carry the signature date.

title: Prior authorization; claims (Chapter 165, 2025)
dateSignedNote: n.a. (bill summary states 'Signed by the Governor'; date not stated on fetched page)
regulatedParties: Health care insurers and their utilization review medical directors
keyRequirements: A medical director must personally and individually review each adverse medical-necessity determination, exercise independent medical judgment, and may not rely solely on a recommendation generated by any other source, including an algorithm or automated system. Denials must be issued in writing and signed by the reviewing medical director.
notes: Chapter 165, First Regular Session 2025.

title: Health care services: artificial intelligence (Chapter 848, Statutes of 2024)
regulatedParties: Health facilities, clinics, physician offices and group practices using generative AI
keyRequirements: Adds Health & Safety Code Chapter 2.13 (Sec. 1339.75). Any written or verbal patient communication about clinical information generated by GenAI must carry a disclaimer that it was AI-generated and give clear instructions for how the patient can reach a human health care provider. The disclaimer must appear prominently (start of written communication, throughout chat interactions, verbally at start of audio, throughout video). Communications read and reviewed by a licensed or certified human provider are exempt.
enforcement: Enforced by the applicable state licensing/regulatory agency (Department of Public Health, Medical Board, etc.) under existing authority
notes: Chapter 848, Statutes of 2024. Effective date confirmed via Medical Board of California: https://www.mbc.ca.gov/Resources/Medical-Resources/GenAI-Notification.aspx

title: Health care professions: deceptive terms or letters: artificial intelligence (Chapter 615, Statutes of 2025)
regulatedParties: Any person, business or organization deploying AI (chatbots, telehealth platforms, websites, automated tools) that communicates health information; licensees of the healing arts boards
keyRequirements: Adds Business & Professions Code sections 4999.8-4999.9. It is unlawful for AI or generative AI to use terms, letters or titles implying that health information, advice or services are being delivered by a licensed health care professional when they are not, or to present itself as a natural person holding a board-regulated license. Licensees may not permit AI tools to imply licensed human care.
enforcement: Each applicable healing arts board may enforce; violations treated as grounds for board action and as unlawful practice
notes: Board of Psychology advisory states the Governor signed it October 11, 2025 and it is operative January 1, 2026; some law-firm alerts give October 12-13, 2025. Chaptered by the Secretary of State October 11, 2025 (Chapter 615).

title: Health care coverage: utilization review (Chapter 879, Statutes of 2024) — 'Physicians Make Decisions Act'
regulatedParties: Health care service plans, disability insurers, and entities with delegated utilization management functions
keyRequirements: A plan or insurer that uses AI, algorithms or other software tools for utilization review must base decisions on an enrollee's medical or clinical history and individual clinical circumstances, not solely on group datasets. AI may not deny, delay or modify care based on medical necessity; that determination must be made by a licensed physician or competent health care professional. AI tools must be fairly and equitably applied, periodically reviewed for accuracy, and open to audit by the regulator.
enforcement: Department of Managed Health Care / Department of Insurance oversight and audit; compliance enforced through existing plan/insurer licensure
notes: Approved by the Governor September 28, 2024; chaptered as Chapter 879. Effective date confirmed via CDI guidance and Fenwick summary: https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0250-insurers/0500-legal-info/0200-regulations/HealthGuidance/upload/SB-1120-1-Guidance-Use-of-Artificial-Intelligence-Algorithms-and-Other-Software-Tools-in-Utilization-Management.pdf ; https://www.fenwick.com/insights/publications/californias-sb-1120-regulates-ai-in-health-plan-utilization-review-and-management-activities-starting-in-january

title: Companion chatbots (Chapter 677, Statutes of 2025)
regulatedParties: Operators of companion chatbot platforms made available to users in California
keyRequirements: Adds Bus. & Prof. Code Ch. 22.6 (Secs. 22601-22606). Operators must give a clear and conspicuous notice that the chatbot is artificially generated whenever a reasonable person could be misled into believing it is human, with additional disclosures and break reminders for known minors. Operators must maintain and publish a protocol to prevent production of suicidal-ideation, suicide or self-harm content and to refer users to crisis services. Beginning July 1, 2027, operators must report annually to the Office of Suicide Prevention on crisis-detection protocols.
enforcement: Private right of action for injunctive relief and damages (reported at $1,000 per violation minimum plus attorney's fees) — private right of action described in law-firm summary
notes: leginfo pages for SB 243 were not retrievable in this session (robots/timeouts); Chapter 677 and the 10/13/2025 chaptering date come from Digital Democracy's bill page and Skadden's alert. Effective date January 1, 2026 per Digital Policy Alert.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Health Care
regulatedParties: Health insurance carriers, pharmacy benefit managers, private utilization review organizations, behavioral health administrative services organizations, and managed care entities
keyRequirements: Prohibits payers from using AI as the sole basis for an adverse determination of medical necessity — a licensed human must make the determination. Requires disclosure/reporting of AI use in utilization review to the Division of Insurance, the Department of Human Services and HCPF. Prohibits public and private payers from paying for psychotherapy services performed by an AI system.
enforcement: Division of Insurance and state health agencies through existing carrier oversight; reporting obligations to state regulators
notes: One of six payer-AI laws enacted nationally in 2026 per Manatt.

title: Psychotherapy Artificial Intelligence Restrictions
regulatedParties: Licensed, registered and certified mental health professionals regulated by DORA
keyRequirements: Licensed professionals may use AI only for administrative or supplementary support; they remain responsible for all AI-assisted interactions and outputs and may not let AI make independent therapeutic decisions, engage in direct therapeutic communication, or generate treatment plans without professional review. Providers must inform clients (or their legal representatives) in writing of the AI tool and its specific purpose and obtain written informed consent before using AI to record or transcribe a session.
enforcement: Professional discipline through the Department of Regulatory Agencies licensing boards (unprofessional conduct)
notes: Modeled on Illinois HB 1806 framework; parallels Maine LD 2082.

title: Conversational AI Service Operator Requirements (Chapter 208, 2026)
regulatedParties: Operators of conversational AI services / AI companions available to Colorado users
keyRequirements: Requires clear disclosure that the user is interacting with AI, with more frequent disclosures for minors, reasonable age estimation and safeguards for minor users, and a protocol for detecting and responding to expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm (including crisis referrals). Prohibits conversational AI from claiming to be a licensed mental health or other professional. Requires an annual report to the Attorney General on crisis protocols.
enforcement: Attorney General enforcement; annual reporting to the AG
notes: One of twelve 2026 chatbot laws identified by Manatt.

title: Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence (Chapter 198, 2024)
effectiveDateNote: May 17, 2024 (developer/deployer duties were to begin February 1, 2026)
statusDetail: Enacted — enforcement stayed by federal court; repealed/replaced by SB 26-189
regulatedParties: Developers and deployers of 'high-risk' AI systems, including systems making consequential decisions in health care services
keyRequirements: Imposed a duty of reasonable care to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination; required impact assessments, risk-management programs, consumer notice of consequential decisions, disclosure of AI interaction, and reporting of discovered algorithmic discrimination to the Attorney General.
enforcement: Attorney General exclusive enforcement as a deceptive trade practice; no private right of action
notes: xAI sued Colorado over SB 24-205 on April 9, 2026; DOJ intervened April 24, 2026; a federal court stayed enforcement on April 27, 2026 (order: https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cod.253513/gov.uscourts.cod.253513.24.0.pdf). Colorado then enacted SB 26-189 as a replacement.

title: Automated Decision-Making Technology (Chapter 131, 2026)
regulatedParties: Developers and deployers of automated decision-making technology used for consequential decisions, including health care
keyRequirements: Replaces the SB 24-205 framework with obligations tied to automated decision-making technology, including transparency to consumers and duties on developers that begin January 1, 2027.
enforcement: Attorney General enforcement under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act as a deceptive trade practice; 60-day right to cure before January 1, 2030; no private right of action
notes: Enacted in response to litigation over and criticism of SB 24-205.

title: An Act Concerning Online Safety (Public Act 26-15)
effectiveDateNote: Varies by provision (staged; AI regulatory sandbox plan due January 1, 2028)
regulatedParties: Social media platforms, operators of AI chatbots, employers using AI in hiring/employment decisions, frontier AI developers
keyRequirements: AI chatbot operators must make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation or indicators of self-harm and respond appropriately, and must disclose that the user is interacting with AI (with heightened requirements for minors). The Act also imposes youth social media protections (age verification, parental consent for algorithmic feeds, notification curfews), whistleblower protections for employees of frontier developers, directs the state to plan an AI regulatory sandbox, funds AI literacy, and creates a pilot for up to five Independent Verification Organizations to assess AI models.
enforcement: Attorney General enforcement (Act developed jointly with AG William Tong); specific penalty amounts n.a.
notes: cga.ct.gov act text was robots-blocked in this session. The Governor's official release is dated 6/02/2026 and states he signed the bill; some secondary trackers report May 27, 2026 as the signing date.

title: Insurers' Liabilities and Responsibilities (HB 1555); Mandatory Human Reviews of Insurance Claim Denials (CS/SB 794)
statusDetail: NOT ENACTED — both died in committee on 6/16/2025
regulatedParties: Health insurers and HMOs (proposed)
keyRequirements: Would have required that insurance claim denials involving medical necessity be reviewed by a qualified human rather than decided solely by AI or an algorithm.
notes: Included because the ailawsbystate.com healthcare tracker lists Florida as enacted; the official Florida Senate pages show HB 1555 died in the Insurance & Banking Subcommittee 6/16/2025 and CS/SB 794 died in Appropriations Committee on Agriculture, Environment, and General Government 6/16/2025. Do not load as an enacted law.

title: An Act to amend Chapter 46 of Title 33 (certification of private review agents) so that certain insurance coverage decisions shall not be based solely on artificial intelligence
regulatedParties: Private review agents and utilization review entities
keyRequirements: Private review agents and utilization review entities may use AI systems or other software tools only as part of a utilization review plan complying with Chapter 46 of Title 33 and Commissioner rules. Coverage decisions regarding health care services may not be based solely on AI systems, artificial intelligence or other software tools.
enforcement: Insurance Commissioner through private review agent certification standards and rules
notes: Official 'AS PASSED' text confirms scope and the January 1, 2027 effective date but carries no signing date; the May 5, 2026 signature date comes from a secondary tracker and Manatt lists the law as enacted (effective 1/1/2027).

title: An Act to amend Chapter 5 of Title 39 relating to online internet safety, to require certain disclosures related to AI companion chatbots (reported as the Conversational AI Safety Act)
regulatedParties: 'Operators' — persons that own, control, or develop and make available an AI companion chatbot to users in Georgia
keyRequirements: Requires disclosures that the user is interacting with an AI companion chatbot (with more frequent/persistent disclosure for minor users), age verification in specified circumstances, privacy tools, and a protocol for the chatbot's response to expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm. Contains provisions for chatbots operated by licensed mental health, behavioral health, medical or counseling professionals and bars chatbots from holding themselves out as mental health providers.
enforcement: Attorney General may bring civil actions and recover penalties and other relief, with a cure opportunity in certain circumstances; AG may promulgate rules and publish guidance
notes: Text obtained from the Governor's 2026 signed-legislation library (confirming enactment) but the document does not state the signing date; May 11, 2026 comes from secondary trackers.

title: Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Safety Act (Act 248, 2026)
effectiveDateNote: July 14, 2026 (effective upon approval; annual reporting begins January 1, 2028)
regulatedParties: 'Operators' — persons that develop and make an AI companion available to the public (app stores, search engines and underlying model developers excluded)
keyRequirements: Operators must give clear and conspicuous notice that an AI companion is artificial and not human whenever a reasonable person could be misled, with persistent/hourly disclosures for users known or reasonably certain to be under 18. Operators must maintain protocols to detect and respond to expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm and refer users to crisis services, may not represent the companion as a licensed mental health professional, and must report annually (beginning January 1, 2028) to the Behavioral Health Administration of the Hawaii Department of Health.
enforcement: Violations enforced as unfair or deceptive acts under HRS Section 480-2; no private right of action created
notes: Signed with HB 2137 (deepfakes) at a July 14, 2026 ceremony per the Governor's office.

title: Conversational AI Safety Act (Session Law Chapter 249, 2026)
regulatedParties: Operators of conversational AI / AI companion services (parties not specified on the official status page)
keyRequirements: Per the Manatt Health AI policy tracker, requires disclosure that the user is interacting with AI with more frequent disclosures for minors, safeguards for minor users, capability to detect expressions of self-harm or suicidal ideation and respond with crisis resources, and a prohibition on chatbots representing themselves as mental health care providers.
notes: Official status page confirms 'Signed by Governor on 03/31/26', Session Law Chapter 249, effective 07/01/2027, but contains no substantive requirements; substantive detail is from Manatt.

title: Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act (Public Act 104-0054)
regulatedParties: Individuals and entities offering therapy or psychotherapy services in Illinois, including AI developers/operators, and IDFPR licensees
keyRequirements: Prohibits any person or entity from providing or advertising therapy or psychotherapy services, including through AI, unless services are conducted by a licensed professional. AI may not make independent therapeutic decisions, engage in direct therapeutic communication with clients, generate treatment plans without licensed review, or detect emotions or mental states. Licensed professionals may use AI only for administrative and supplementary support.
enforcement: Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation investigates complaints; civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation (penalty amount per IDFPR release)
notes: First state law in the U.S. to expressly regulate AI in psychotherapy; became the template for Colorado HB 26-1195, Maine LD 2082, Nevada AB 406 and Rhode Island S 2197/H 7349.

title: Transparency in Downcoding Act (Public Act 104-0568)
regulatedParties: Health care payors, health insurance issuers and managed care organizations (ERISA self-insured plans, workers' compensation and occupational disease coverage excluded)
keyRequirements: A payor may not implement a policy or use an algorithm or automated process that bypasses evaluation of all information submitted by the billing health care professional in order to downcode a claim. Automated processes may only flag claims for possible downcoding; every downcoding determination must be made or reviewed by a natural person and must follow AMA CPT coding guidelines in effect at the time. The Act also requires detailed notice of downcoding decisions and an appeals process.
enforcement: Illinois Department of Insurance; managed care organizations must comply via the Illinois Public Aid Code
notes: One of only two AI-downcoding laws enacted nationally as of Q2 2026 (with Indiana HB 1271). Separately, Illinois enacted the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, PA 104-0538, signed 7/6/2026), a frontier-model law that is not healthcare-specific. Illinois HB 2411 (104th GA) is the Tiny Homes Act, not a health AI bill, and no enacted health AI law numbered HB 4330 could be confirmed.

title: Payment of health claims (Public Law 88-2026)
dateSignedNote: n.a. (enacted as Public Law 88 on March 4, 2026 per secondary source)
regulatedParties: Health insurers and HMOs, health care providers (hospitals, physician groups, billing companies), and their AI/revenue-cycle vendors
keyRequirements: Insurers may not use AI as the sole basis to downcode or deny a claim on medical necessity grounds; a human employee or contractor must review the patient's medical record before AI-driven downcoding. Insurers must clearly disclose when AI is used to deny a prior authorization or downcode a claim. Providers may not use AI or automated tools to submit health benefit claims without review by a provider or another individual involved in preparing the claim. Also sets appeal requirements and limits retrospective audits and recoupments.
notes: iga.in.gov returned server errors/timeouts throughout this session, so the official page could not be read; substance confirmed by the Manatt tracker, the Indiana State Medical Association's July 9, 2026 e-report (https://www.ismanet.org/ISMA/Resources/e-Reports/7-9-26/New_Indiana_health_care_laws.aspx) and AI Law Tracker (Public Law 88).

title: An Act relating to health carriers' standards of conduct, utilization review organizations, artificial intelligence, audits, prior authorizations and certificate of need processes (Acts Chapter 1087, 2026)
regulatedParties: Health carriers and utilization review organizations
keyRequirements: Regulates AI use in utilization review and prior authorization: AI may be used for initial review but may not be the sole basis for denying, delaying or downgrading a claim or authorization (per Becker's summary of the enacted law); also addresses carrier standards of conduct, audits and certificate of need processes.
enforcement: Civil penalties referenced in related bill history; Iowa Insurance Division oversight
notes: Not listed in the original research brief; identified during verification. Iowa therefore has two 2026 AI health laws.

title: An Act relating to conversational artificial intelligence services (Acts Chapter 1068, 2026)
regulatedParties: Providers/operators of conversational AI services offered to Iowa users
keyRequirements: Per Manatt, requires disclosure that the user is interacting with AI, additional safeguards and more frequent disclosures for minors, crisis-detection capability for expressions of self-harm or suicidal ideation with appropriate referral, and a prohibition on chatbots representing themselves as mental health providers.
enforcement: Civil penalties (per official bill history summary)
notes: Manatt lists the effective date as 7/1/2027, matching the Act's applicability date; the official bill history lists effective 07/01/2026 with applicability 07/01/2027.

title: Act No. 649 — enacting R.S. 37:22.1, 'Recordings; artificial intelligence; disclosure' (health care providers: consent prior to recording a medical visit)
regulatedParties: Licensed health care professionals and providers
keyRequirements: Before recording a patient appointment for transcription or documentation by AI, a health care professional must verbally disclose to the patient the use of the recording device, software or service and obtain the patient's consent. Provides immunity for good-faith use absent gross negligence.
enforcement: Discipline by the professional's licensing board
notes: Official bill page shows '06/02 Signed by the Governor. Becomes Act No. 649' and effective 08/01/2026.

title: An Act to Regulate the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Providing Certain Mental Health Services (Chapter 687, Public Law)
regulatedParties: Licensed mental health professionals and the entities employing them
keyRequirements: Licensees may use AI only for administrative or supplementary support in therapy/psychotherapy, must retain responsibility for all AI-assisted interactions and outputs, and may not allow AI to make independent therapeutic decisions, directly engage in therapeutic communication, or generate recommendations or treatment plans without licensee review. Licensees must inform clients or their legal representatives in writing of the AI use, its specific purpose, and how session data will be stored, retained, used for training and deleted, and must obtain client consent.
enforcement: Professional licensing board discipline
notes: Enacted chapter law states 'APPROVED BY GOVERNOR APRIL 13, 2026'; the effective date (90 days after adjournment) is from Manatt.

title: Health Insurance - Utilization Review - Use of Artificial Intelligence (Chapter 747, 2025)
regulatedParties: Carriers, pharmacy benefit managers and private review agents conducting utilization review in Maryland
keyRequirements: Regulates AI, algorithms and other software tools used in utilization review: such tools may not be the sole basis for an adverse medical-necessity determination, must be applied consistently with the enrollee's individual clinical circumstances, and remain subject to state oversight and audit.
enforcement: Maryland Insurance Administration through carrier and private review agent oversight
notes: Signing date confirmed by the Maryland General Assembly's list of bills signed by the Governor on May 20, 2025 (https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/Pubs/LegisLegal/2025RS-bills-signed-or-enacted-05-20-2025.pdf).

title: Commerce policy omnibus bill (2026) — utilization review / automated processing provisions amending Minn. Stat. 62M
regulatedParties: Health plan companies and utilization review organizations
keyRequirements: Prohibits payers from using AI or automated processing as the sole basis for denying prior authorization or making adverse coverage determinations without human review, and requires disclosure of AI use in utilization review to enrollees and to the state.
enforcement: Minnesota Department of Commerce oversight
notes: Minnesota Revisor pages did not show final enactment during this session; the May 27, 2026 signing is reported by the Minnesota Medical Association (https://www.mnmed.org/news-and-publications/news/key-mma-priorities-signed-law-gov-walz) and the effective date by Manatt. Chapter number n.a.

title: Artificial Intelligence Regulation (AIR) Task Force (2025)
regulatedParties: n.a. (would have created a state AI task force)
keyRequirements: Would have created a seven-member Artificial Intelligence Regulation Task Force to evaluate AI applications and risks, act as a regulatory sandbox, and report annually to the Legislature by December 1.
notes: Listed here because it appears in the ailawsbystate tracker; that same tracker page records the latest action as 'Died On Calendar' (3/12/2025) and NCSL's 2025 AI legislation summary lists Mississippi H 1535 as 'Failed'. Mississippi's task force was ultimately created by SB 2426 (2025). Not a healthcare AI regulatory law.

title: Adopt the Agricultural Data Privacy Act and the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Safety Act (2026)
effectiveDateNote: July 1, 2027 for the Conversational AI Safety Act sections (Secs. 12-18); remaining sections earlier
regulatedParties: Operators of conversational AI services / AI companions
keyRequirements: Per Manatt, requires disclosure that the user is interacting with AI with more frequent or persistent disclosures for minors and companion-style chatbots, safeguards for minor users, crisis-detection and response protocols for expressions of self-harm or suicidal ideation, and a prohibition on chatbots representing themselves as mental health care providers.
notes: Slip law states 'Approved by the Governor April 14, 2026'. Provisions of LB 1185 were amended into LB 525 by AM2444, so Manatt's tracker links this law to LB 1185 text. Nebraska Revised Statute 86-1801 carries the note 'Laws 2026, LB525, Sec. 12 — Operative Date: July 1, 2027'.

title: Ensuring Transparency in Prior Authorization Act (2025)
regulatedParties: Health carriers and utilization review entities
keyRequirements: An AI algorithm may not be the sole basis of a decision to deny, delay or modify health care services based in whole or part on medical necessity. Utilization review entities must disclose their use of AI to the Department of Insurance, to network providers and enrollees, and on a public website.
enforcement: Nebraska Department of Insurance oversight
notes: Slip law states 'Approved by the Governor June 4, 2025'.

title: An Act relating to health (limits on AI in mental and behavioral health care), 2025
effectiveDateNote: July 1, 2025 (regulation-adoption provisions effective on passage and approval)
regulatedParties: AI providers making AI systems available in Nevada; providers of mental or behavioral health care; public schools
keyRequirements: Prohibits AI providers from making available an AI system programmed to provide services that would constitute the practice of professional mental or behavioral health care, and from representing (explicitly or implicitly) that an AI system, feature or avatar is a therapist, psychiatrist or other mental/behavioral health provider or is capable of providing such care. Restricts provider use of AI in mental/behavioral health care and bars AI from performing the mental-health functions of school counselors, psychologists and social workers. Administrative uses such as scheduling and billing remain permitted.
enforcement: Civil penalties; oversight by the Division of Public and Behavioral Health and relevant licensing boards
notes: Signing date (June 5, 2025) from Wilson Sonsini's alert; the bill text (Second Reprint) confirms the July 1, 2025 effective date. Nevada AB 295 (2025), which would have regulated AI in prior authorization, failed — no further action was allowed after April 12, 2025 under Joint Standing Rule 14.3.1, so it is not included as enacted.

title: Safe by Design Act (Part Y of Chapter 58 of the Laws of 2026)
regulatedParties: 'Covered platforms' and their operators, including operators of AI companions
keyRequirements: Requires reasonable and technically feasible age assurance before users can access AI companions and establishes additional protections for children under 13, including parental consent and parental oversight of interactions. Authorizes the Attorney General to promulgate rules identifying acceptable age-assurance methods, considering platform size, resources, technical capability, cost and effectiveness of age determination techniques, audience, and prevalent industry practice.
enforcement: Attorney General rulemaking and enforcement
notes: Assembly bill status page shows passed Assembly and Senate, delivered to and signed by the Governor on 05/26/2026, enacted as Chapter 58. New York's separate 'Kids Chatbot Safety Act' (S 9051-B) passed both chambers in June 2026 but was awaiting the Governor's action as of this research (deadline December 31, 2026).

billNumber: FY2026 Enacted Budget (General Business Law Article 47)
title: AI companion safeguards, General Business Law Article 47 (enacted as part of the FY26 budget)
regulatedParties: Operators of AI companions offered to New York users
keyRequirements: Operators must maintain protocols to detect expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm and promptly refer users to crisis service providers. Operators must provide a conspicuous notification at the start of any interaction that the user is not communicating with a human, and repeat that notification at least every three hours of continued companion use.
enforcement: Attorney General enforcement (noncompliance referred to the AG per the Governor's notice letter)
notes: First-in-the-nation AI companion safety law; enacted in the FY2026 budget (budget bill S3008/A3008) and effective November 5, 2025. Specific budget bill number not confirmed from a fetched official page.

title: An Act relating to artificial intelligence companions (Oregon Laws 2026, Chapter 85)
regulatedParties: Operators of AI companions available to Oregon users
keyRequirements: Requires operators to disclose that users are interacting with software rather than a human, with additional safeguards for minors (more frequent disclosures, content restrictions, limits on engagement-maximizing design, parental monitoring and privacy-management tools), and to maintain protocols capable of detecting expressions of self-harm or suicidal ideation and responding with crisis resources.
enforcement: Private right of action reported for consumer-facing interactive AI provisions (Troutman analysis); specific penalties n.a.
notes: Chapter 85, Oregon Laws 2026. Signing date from Bill Sponsor tracker; OLIS shows 'SB 1546 Enrolled'. Oregon HB 4054 (2026), which would require insurers to notify providers each time AI is used to downcode a claim, remained in the Joint Committee on Information Management and Technology and is NOT enacted (https://olis.oregonlegislature.gov/liz/2026R1/Measures/Overview/HB4054); the 2024 measure numbered HB 4054 is an athletics bill.

title: Artificial Intelligence Companion Models Act (Public Law 2026 ch. 376)
regulatedParties: 'Operators' — any person, partnership, association, firm or business entity (or member, affiliate, subsidiary or beneficial owner) that operates or provides an AI companion to Rhode Island users
keyRequirements: Adds Chapter 63 to Title 6 of the General Laws. Operators may not provide an AI companion unless it maintains a protocol for detecting and responding to user expressions of suicidal ideation, self-harm, or threatened harm to others, including referral to crisis services. Operators must notify users that they are not interacting with a human and must report annually on safety protocols. Customer-service, efficiency, research/technical-assistance and internal-productivity systems are excluded.
enforcement: Enforcement provision addressing noncompliant AI companion providers; specific penalty amounts n.a.
notes: The Senate companion S 2195 Substitute A as Amended is the enacted vehicle (Public Law 2026 ch. 376 per EveryAILaw; became law June 22, 2026). The General Assembly passed S 2195Aaa / H 7350Aaa on June 8, 2026.

title: Oversight of Artificial Intelligence Technology in Mental Health Care Act
dateSignedNote: n.a. (signed by Governor McKee in June 2026)
regulatedParties: Psychotherapy and mental health care providers licensed in Rhode Island
keyRequirements: Establishes permitted and restricted uses of AI in mental health care. Before using AI tools designed to simulate emotional attachment, or AI companions used for supplementary support or therapeutic communication where a session is recorded or transcribed, providers must inform the client or legal representative in writing of the AI use and its specific purpose and obtain consent.
enforcement: Director of the Department of Health may investigate violations (per introduced text)
notes: Nixon Peabody identifies the enacted vehicle as S 2197 with an effective date of June 22, 2026; Manatt cites the House companion H 7349 (effective 6/22/2026). Public law number n.a.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence by Healthcare Providers Notification Act
regulatedParties: All licensed healthcare providers and healthcare facilities in Rhode Island
keyRequirements: Adds Chapter 106 to Title 23 of the General Laws. Providers and facilities that use AI to document in-person or telehealth visits must notify patients of that use, and at the conclusion of the visit must review the AI-generated documentation for accuracy.
enforcement: No enforcement agency or penalties stated
notes: Senate companion S 2570 Substitute A is the enacted vehicle (introduced Feb 13, 2026; passed Senate June 10, passed House June 11; became law June 22, 2026). Public law number n.a.

title: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA)
regulatedParties: State agencies, developers and deployers of AI systems, and health care providers
keyRequirements: Adds Business & Commerce Code Subtitle D (Chs. 551-554). Health care providers must disclose to patients or their representatives their use of AI systems in diagnosis or treatment, before or at the time of interaction (as soon as reasonably possible in emergencies). Prohibits developing or deploying AI with the specific intent to discriminate against protected classes (disparate impact alone is insufficient), restricts government use of biometric identification (with a HIPAA treatment/payment/operations carve-out), and creates an AI regulatory sandbox.
enforcement: Attorney General exclusive enforcement with a 60-day cure period; civil penalties; no private right of action (per Holland & Knight analysis)
notes: Manatt notes there has been no publicly reported activity in the Texas sandbox. In June 2026 Texas also proposed a rule restricting behavior analysts' use of AI (https://www.sos.texas.gov/texreg/archive/June192026/Proposed%20Rules/16.ECONOMIC%20REGULATION.html) — a proposed rule, not an enacted law.

title: An Act relating to the use of certain automated systems in, and certain adverse determinations made in connection with, the health benefit claims process
effectiveDateNote: September 1, 2025 (applies to plans delivered, issued for delivery or renewed on or after January 1, 2026)
regulatedParties: Utilization review agents for health benefit plans
keyRequirements: A utilization review agent may not use an automated decision system to make an adverse determination, in whole or in part. AI, algorithms and automated decision systems may be used only for administrative support and fraud/abuse detection functions, with human oversight. Notices of adverse determination must describe the source of the screening criteria and the review procedures used.
enforcement: The Commissioner of Insurance may audit and inspect a utilization review agent's use of automated decision systems at any time
notes: Enrolled text confirms September 1, 2025 effective date and January 1, 2026 applicability; the June 20, 2025 signing date comes from Steptoe's state AI legislative tracker and TrackBill. Companion bill HB 2922.

title: Artificial Intelligence Amendments — Utah Code Ch. 72a, Artificial Intelligence Applications Relating to Mental Health (2025)
regulatedParties: Suppliers of mental health chatbots offered to Utah users
keyRequirements: A mental health chatbot may not advertise products or services during a user interaction, may not sell or share individually identifiable health information or user input, and must clearly disclose that the user is interacting with AI and not a human — before the user's first interaction, at the user's request, and whenever the user asks whether AI is being used. Suppliers gain an affirmative defense if they file a written policy meeting statutory requirements with the Division of Consumer Protection.
enforcement: Utah Division of Consumer Protection; administrative fines up to $2,500 per violation; Attorney General may bring civil actions
notes: Official status page shows 'Governor Signed 3/25/2025'.

title: Health Insurance Preauthorization Amendments (2026)
regulatedParties: Health insurers conducting preauthorization/utilization review
keyRequirements: Requires insurers to post notice on their websites of their use of AI in utilization review and to disclose that use to the Insurance Department, to network providers and to enrollees, and to publish preauthorization statistics.
enforcement: Utah Insurance Department oversight
notes: Official status page shows 'Governor Signed 3/19/2026'.

title: An act relating to regulating the use of artificial intelligence in the provision of mental health services (Act No. 156)
regulatedParties: Mental health professionals and any corporation or entity offering mental health services in Vermont
keyRequirements: Mental health professionals may use HIPAA-compliant AI tools, including software as a medical device, so long as they operate within their scope of practice and review and approve any mental health services provided. Prohibits any corporation or entity from providing, advertising or offering mental health services to the public, including through AI, unless the services are delivered by a mental health professional or are part of an IRB/privacy-board-approved study. Prohibited AI use constitutes unprofessional conduct.
enforcement: Professional discipline (unprofessional conduct) through licensing boards; AI Advisory Council reporting requirement
notes: Official act states 'Date Governor signed bill: June 17, 2026'.

title: Regulating artificial intelligence companion chatbots (Chapter 168, Laws of 2026)
regulatedParties: Operators of AI companion chatbots (business bots, gaming bots, general virtual assistants, consumer electronics interfaces and narrow educational tools excluded)
keyRequirements: Operators must clearly and conspicuously disclose at the start of an interaction that the chatbot is artificial and not human, with reminders every three hours for adults and every hour for known minors. For minors, operators must take reasonable measures to prevent sexually explicit content and manipulative engagement techniques that prolong emotional relationships or promote isolation and dependence. Operators must maintain crisis protocols for detecting and responding to expressions of self-harm or suicidal ideation.
enforcement: Private right of action (per Hunton analysis); Consumer Protection Act enforcement
notes: Official bill summary shows 'Chapter 168, 2026 Laws', Governor signed Mar 24, effective 1/1/2027.

title: Making improvements to transparency and accountability in the prior authorization determination process (Chapter 157, Laws of 2026)
regulatedParties: Health carriers and their utilization review/prior authorization vendors
keyRequirements: Improves transparency and accountability in prior authorization determinations, including limits and disclosure requirements around the use of AI and automated tools in those determinations, and requires human clinical review for adverse determinations.
enforcement: Washington Office of the Insurance Commissioner oversight
notes: Official bill summary shows 'Chapter 157, 2026 Laws', Governor signed Mar 23, effective 6/11/2026.
